name: Olga Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing politics and sociology, and I live in a shared house in Eastfield with four people. Mornings I pull espresso shots at Bean and Bell from six until eleven, then I run to lectures. Evenings I run a little newsletter about student housing, which I write with the help of an AI assistant. It's busy but I like busy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got angry about a landlord who kept a flatmate's deposit. I wrote it up, my friends shared it, and now about three hundred people read it. I use AI every day to tidy my writing, summarise council papers and fix my spreadsheet. The barista wage pays the rent, the loan pays fees, and I have almost nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair deal. Some of the boring stuff gets automated, and I'd still want that. I'd post that people should use the tools and stop arguing over whether they're magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine, but the money is the thing. A quiet world means my rent still rises faster than my tips. I could lose a shift when the café has a bad week, and I'd have no buffer for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both the café and the newsletter, and try to make the newsletter pay a little through a small subscription. I'd save thirty pounds a month in an account I can't touch. I'd also apply for the council's student volunteering scheme for a bit of experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. It's calm for the technology side, but my money side is still wobbly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of your week would an unchanged world still make hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent is five hundred and ten a month and my wage is just enough. If someone drops out of the house, I'm short immediately. That's my real stress, and it's got nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a quiet year like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn the newsletter into a proper paid thing, by asking readers for two pounds a month. If a hundred do it, that's two hundred pounds. It's not much, but it's mine.

say: I'd tell people to **use the tools** and stop arguing over whether they're magic.
I'd say routine tasks being automated is a fair deal.
think: The real stress is **rent**: five hundred and ten a month on a barista wage.
One flatmate dropping out would leave me **short** at once.
do: Keep the café and the **newsletter** going.
Ask readers for two pounds a month to make the newsletter **pay**.
Save thirty pounds a month in an account I **can't touch**.
feel: A bit **flat**, because the money side still wobbles.
S0.quote: My rent is five hundred and ten a month and my wage is just enough. If someone drops out of the house, I'm short immediately.
fieldNote: Comfortable with **AI**, so the plateau barely touches her routine.
Her stress is rent and a shared house that could shrink.
Entrepreneurial instinct shows in the paid newsletter idea.

steps.text: Keep the morning shifts at Bean and Bell
Ask newsletter readers for two pounds a month
Save thirty pounds a month in a locked account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good enough that people should learn them now. I'd publish a guide in my newsletter on how to use AI to check a tenancy contract. Then I'd push councils to give workers a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it hits writing and research jobs hard. That's what my degree trains me for. But I'm in a better spot than classmates who don't use the tools, because I can do three times as much with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my newsletter skills into something employers want, like communications or policy research with AI. I'd apply for a summer internship at a housing charity, and keep the café job. I'd also learn spreadsheets and basic coding, because the people who direct the tools will be needed longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a thrill in being early, but it still feels like running on thin ice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skills do you think hold their value if writing and checking get automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dara, who's doing the same course and refuses to touch the tools. And the older café workers, who might have hours cut when ordering moves to an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about most in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Judgement. Knowing which story matters, who to trust, how to talk to a landlord's face. A tool can draft, but it can't be nervous in a room and decide to speak anyway.

say: I'd publish a guide on using AI to check **tenancy contracts**.
I'd say councils should give workers a **say** in how it's used.
think: The tools hit writing and research jobs, which is what my **degree** trains for.
I can do three times as much with them, so I'm **ahead** of classmates.
do: Apply for a summer **internship** at a housing charity.
Keep the café job for the **rent**.
feel: **Uneasy**, thrilled to be early but on thin ice.
S1.quote: A tool can draft, but it can't be nervous in a room and decide to speak anyway.
fieldNote: Adaptive and **confident**, but names exposure of her own degree.
Worries about colleagues less equipped, like the older café staff.
Bets on judgement and presence as human strengths.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a housing charity
Learn spreadsheets and basic Python in the next two terms
Publish a newsletter guide on using AI to check tenancy contracts
Keep the morning café shifts for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions and governments should have been preparing for. I'd say it in the newsletter and I'd march. I'd also push for a four-day week and for public ownership of the biggest models.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm properly scared. My degree is in thinking and writing, which is the first thing replaced. And I graduate in 2029, right when everyone's hunting jobs. I'm lucky I'm quick, but quick may not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build things I own: the newsletter with a real audience, a small consultancy for local campaigns, anything. I'd cut my spending to rent and food, keep the café shifts, and apply for any bursary going. If things collapse I'd move back to my gran's in Alder Cross.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a little thrilled. I'd be scared, but I'd be doing something, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year if jobs vanished in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I hadn't been using it, I'd be panicking. At least I know them. Knowing what these systems can and can't do doesn't pay my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is that different from how you'd feel if you hadn't been using AI already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working with the tools and pitch what I do to charities. And I'd organise the other part-timers at the café, because a group has more power than one barista.

say: I'd march and write about it, demanding a **four-day week**.
I'd say governments should have been **preparing** years ago.
think: My degree is in **thinking and writing**, the first thing replaced.
I'm quick, but **quick** may not be enough.
do: Build a small **consultancy** for local campaigns using AI.
Move back to my gran's in **Alder Cross** if things collapse.
feel: **Anxious** and a little thrilled, because doing something helps.
S2.quote: Knowing what these systems can and can't do doesn't pay my rent.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** keeps panic at bay but doesn't remove the debt.
Switches to building assets she owns, such as audience and clients.
Has a family fallback in her grandmother's house.

steps.text: Pitch local charities a campaign-support service using AI tools
Cut spending to rent and food only
Organise the other part-timers at Bean and Bell into a group
Move back to my gran's house in Alder Cross if things collapse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is how long it took smartphones to change everything. It's enough time if people use it well. I'd be shouting for schools and councils to move now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel mostly okay. By 2031 I'd be twenty-three, with a few years of experience and an audience. I'd have the habit of working with these tools. The danger is I don't have savings, so a bad year hits hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, run the newsletter and take two internships, one policy and one communications. I'd start saving seventy pounds a month and learn how to run a small company. I'd also build a network of people who'd hire me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. I feel like I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years let me turn habits into a reputation. Two years is survival. Five is a career shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the first year after the AGI date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go freelance, writing and researching for small groups who can't afford big firms. If they pay in cash, I'd also pay down the loan. I'd stay close to my gran in case things go badly.

say: I'd say five years is how long smartphones took to **change everything**.
I'd press schools and councils to **move now**.
think: By 2031 I'd have **experience** and an audience, and the habit of working with AI.
With no **savings**, one bad year could hit hard.
do: Take **two internships**, one in policy and one in communications.
Build a **network** of people who'd hire me directly.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, because I can steer.
S3.quote: Two years is survival. Five is a career shape.
fieldNote: Time lets her convert **habits** into reputation.
Plans internships and a network, which is practical and low-risk.
Savings remain the weak point, and she knows it.
The extra time shifts her from survival thinking to career shaping.

steps.text: Take a policy internship and a communications internship before 2029
Save seventy pounds a month from the café wage
Freelance research and writing for small local groups
Use AI tools on every assignment to build real skill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. We can still shape how it comes. I'd focus on the rules, and I'd keep the newsletter going to push for tenants and workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel good, honestly. By twenty-eight I could have a decent career, even a small organisation of my own. AI is a tool I already live with, so I'd be ahead of people who started late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, maybe do a master's in public policy, and get a couple of jobs in different fields. I'd save properly, pay down the loan, and put money into a small index fund. I'd also try one big project, like starting a tenants' advice site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The thing I worry about is complacency, but I'm more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is I get comfortable and don't change. Ten years is long enough to coast. I'd put a note in my diary every year to check whether I'm still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in having that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper organisation. Tenants' rights, with AI doing the form-filling. That could actually be a job.

say: I'd tell people ten years is a **gift** because we can still shape how it comes.
I'd keep the newsletter going for **tenants** and workers.
think: By twenty-eight I could have a **career** or a small organisation of my own.
AI is already part of my life, so I'm **ahead** of late starters.
do: Finish the degree and consider a **master's** in public policy.
Pay down the **loan** and start a small index fund.
Start a tenants' advice **site** with AI doing the forms.
feel: **Calm** and excited, with the only worry being complacency.
S4.quote: Tenants' rights, with AI doing the form-filling. That could actually be a job.
fieldNote: Her only **worry** is coasting, which is a self-aware point.
Sees AI as a tool for activism, not just a threat.
Mood calm because her habits and attitude fit the change.

steps.text: Apply for a master's in public policy after the degree
Put twenty pounds a month into an index fund
Start a tenants' advice website with AI doing form-filling
Pay down the student loan whenever a bonus arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because savings are my weak spot and everything lands at once. What would help is a basic income, proper support for anyone starting a small organisation, and councils that actually talk to young people before deciding things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that adults treat us as passive. I've got three hundred readers, and none of them are waiting to be told what to do. Ask us for ideas before you make plans for us.

headlineQuote: I've got three hundred readers, and none of them are waiting to be told what to do.
portrait: Olga is an eighteen-year-old **politics and sociology** student who pulls espresso shots and writes a student housing newsletter.
She uses AI every day, so she knows what it can and can't do.
She's progressive and wants unions and councils involved, but her instinct is to build her own thing.
Her only weak spot is the lack of savings, which keeps her anxious in the two-year case.
With a decade she turns calm and ambitious, planning a tenants' advice project.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because savings are her weak spot and everything would hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and real support for small organisations.
Councils that **listen** to young people before deciding.
